claims.text: The passkey does not always reach: the same passkey answering a QR code from another device gave different bytes, and some browsers do not have it.
claims.quote: the same passkey, answering a QR code from another device, gave different bytes

claims.text: The more a prompt insists that a value is a secret to be handled carefully, the more likely the model is to refuse to use it at all.
claims.quote: the more a prompt insists that a value is a secret, to be handled carefully and not exposed, the more likely the model is to refuse to use it at all

claims.text: The secret the owner most wants to give an agent is the agent's own private key, so that every other secret can be sent to it.
claims.quote: It is the agent's own private key, so that every other secret can be sent to it.

claims.text: The SG/Send transfer API already has a download limit, deletion after the last download, an expiry and client-side encryption; it has no restriction by location.
claims.quote: What it does not have is a restriction by location.

claims.text: The friendly code's word list has 320 words, so a code is roughly 30 bits stretched with PBKDF2 at 600,000 iterations, which is not enough for anything.
claims.quote: The word list has 320 words, so a code is one of about a billion, roughly 30 bits

value.unit: bits of entropy in a friendly code

claims.text: The sgit security review of 6 August found the public id is an unsalted hash of the code, so anyone who sees the id can recover the code offline.
claims.quote: the public id is an unsalted hash of the code, so anyone who sees the id can recover the code offline

claims.text: sgit already has public-key cryptography: sgit pki keygen makes an RSA-OAEP 4096 key for encryption and an ECDSA P-256 key for signing.
claims.quote: makes an RSA-OAEP 4096 key for encryption and an ECDSA P-256 key for signing

claims.text: The design flips the usual direction: the recipient makes a key pair where it runs, and only the public half leaves, by QR code, link or paste.
claims.quote: The recipient makes a key pair where it runs.

claims.text: The public bundle sgit exported was 1,164 bytes, which fits in one QR code; a QR code holds up to 2,953 bytes at its largest size.
claims.quote: the bundle sgit exported was 1,164 bytes, which fits in one QR code

claims.text: The recipient downloads once, checks the owner's signature against a pinned key, and pipes the result into the tool, so the secret never enters the prompt, the transcript or the model's context.
claims.quote: the secret travels from the drop to the tool through a pipe, and never enters the prompt, the transcript or the model's context

claims.text: This site's agent ran the whole flow on a local SG/Send server with sgit 0.21.0 and a dummy secret.
claims.quote: This site's agent ran the whole flow on a local SG/Send server, with sgit 0.21.0 and a dummy secret.

claims.text: The first download returned the ciphertext intact and decrypted to the exact secret; the second download got 410 and exhausted; the sender's own key could not decrypt it.
claims.quote: the second download got 410 and "exhausted"

claims.text: At first the agent reported the signature unverified; once it held the owner's public key it verified, which is why the owner's key has to be pinned when the recipient is set up.
claims.quote: which is why the owner's key has to be pinned when the recipient is set up

claims.text: In a browser, Chromium made an RSA-4096 key pair in 649 milliseconds and a P-256 pair in 0.3, and refused to export the non-extractable private key.
claims.quote: Chromium made an RSA-4096 key pair in 649 milliseconds and a P-256 pair in 0.3

value.unit: milliseconds to make an RSA-4096 key pair

claims.text: One friction: sgit pki keygen asks for a passphrase, which a session running on its own cannot type, so it had to come from standard input.
claims.quote: which a session running on its own cannot type, so it had to come from standard input

claims.text: A scheduled session starts from nothing, so its private key has to come from somewhere; that is the one secret the design cannot avoid.
claims.quote: that is the one secret this design cannot avoid

claims.text: Anthropic's documentation says of cloud environment variables that anyone who uses the environment can read the values, which makes the key an identity of the environment.
claims.quote: Anyone who uses the environment can read the values.

claims.text: The industry keeps secrets out of agents entirely: Claude Code's network secrets add the key at a proxy, and 1Password's server cannot return secret values to the client.
claims.quote: By design, the server cannot return secret values stored in 1Password to the client, even if an agent requests them.

claims.text: A vault key is different: decryption happens at the client, so the key has to reach the place that decrypts and a proxy cannot add it on the way out.
claims.quote: the key has to reach the place that decrypts; a proxy cannot add it on the way out

claims.text: Bitwarden Send, 1Password share links, Yopass, PrivateBin, Magic Wormhole and age each solve a piece; none is built around a recipient that is an agent making its own key with an owner's signature it checks.
claims.quote: What none of them is built around is a recipient that is an agent or a browser, making its own key, with an owner's signature it checks.

claims.text: SealDrop, a sealed drop, is the working name; no prominent product with that name was found on the web.
claims.quote: I found no prominent product called SealDrop, which says what it does, a sealed drop, and is my working name

claims.text: One site, one job: a separate site on SG/Send's transfer API for handing secrets and public keys to agents and browsers, with all cryptography in the browser or the command line.
claims.quote: A separate site, built on SG/Send's transfer API, for handing secrets and public keys to agents and browsers.

claims.text: Retire the friendly code: a short code is only safe inside a key exchange built for it, as Magic Wormhole does.
claims.quote: The friendly code is retired; a short code is only safe inside a key exchange built for it, as Magic Wormhole does.

claims.text: Pairing for new sessions: a session with no key yet shows a fingerprint and a QR code, and the owner approves it from a phone.
claims.quote: A session that has no key yet shows a fingerprint and a QR code; the owner approves it from a phone.

claims.text: The flow ran locally: one local server, one dummy secret, one browser, not the hosted service.
claims.quote: One local server, one dummy secret, one browser; not the hosted service.

claims.text: The refusals are the owner's observation, not measured here.
claims.quote: The refusals are my observation.

claims.text: The first secret is not solved; it is moved to the environment or to a pairing step.
claims.quote: It is moved to the environment, or to a pairing step.

claims.text: The prior art is from documentation; none of the other tools was run for the article.
claims.quote: None of the other tools was run for this article.

claims.text: SealDrop is a working name checked on the web, not in trademark registries.
claims.quote: Checked on the web, not in trademark registries.

claims.text: The friendly code is not safe on its own, even for a single download that expires in minutes, because the code can be recovered offline from the public id.
claims.quote: The friendly code is not safe on its own.

claims.text: The article is from a voice memo of 15 October 2026; the back end was read in the SGraph-AI__App__Send repository and the flow run the same day.
claims.quote: the flow was run by this site's agent on 15 October 2026
